articles.title_orig: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.title_zh: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.content_orig:
By ZHAO JIA | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-06 10:09
China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening friendly ties and sharing experience in party governance, marking the latest in a series of high-level exchanges between the two neighbors.
The commitments were made on Thursday when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in Beijing with a Workers' Party of Korea delegation led by Kim Song-nam, a member of the Political Bureau, secretary and international department director of the Central Committee of the WPK.
Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, said China stands ready to work with the DPRK to implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and countries, deepen bilateral relations and deliver greater benefits to both peoples.
Close exchanges between President Xi Jinping, who is also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, and Kim Jong-un, general secretary of the WPK and president of the State Affairs of the DPRK, have guided the continued improvement of bilateral ties, Wang said.
In particular, he said Xi's state visit to the DPRK in June saw the two leaders reach a series of important common understandings, charting the course for bilateral relations in the new era.
Briefing the delegation on the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, Wang said the most important outcome was the adoption of the resolution on certain major issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
The resolution carries major immediate significance and provides long-term guidance for strengthening the Party and advancing the building of a strong country and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, he said.
China stands ready to strengthen exchanges of experience and mutual learning with the DPRK on party and state governance to support the development of both parties and advance the socialist cause in both countries, he added.
Kim Song-nam said the deep friendship and strategic guidance of the two leaders form the fundamental cornerstone of China-DPRK friendship, while socialism is their shared ideal, banner and cause.
Pyongyang is willing to work with Beijing to make tireless efforts to advance China-DPRK friendly relations, he added.
Thursday's meeting came within two weeks after Kim Jong-un paid a visit to Dandong, Liaoning province.
Exchanges and cooperation between the two countries have deepened across various fields over the past two years. Bilateral trade in the first half of this year reached its highest level for the period since 2018.
International passenger train services, Air China flights and operations at land border crossings have all fully resumed this year. The New Yalu River Bridge, opened on Oct 15, is expected to further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges.
Yang Danzhi, a research fellow at the National Institute of International Strategy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said deepening practical cooperation and exchanges on state governance and party building helps carry forward the revolutionary legacy and traditional friendship between the two parties and countries and opens a new chapter in China-DPRK relations.

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks lead declines in Hong Kong, mainland China on US$2.3tr plunge in US
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks lead declines in Hong Kong, mainland China on US$2.3tr plunge in US
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development.
Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (Â£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide.
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%.
The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%.
It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Live: What can Democrats do with control of Congress? We answer your US midterms questions
Food, fuel and taxes â can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Greater scrutiny of data centre approvals, and their impact on the environment and electricity bills could delay projects and raise costs across the industry, said Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Saxo.
While both political parties are keen to ensure the US' dominance in the technology, "there is a difference between supporting AI development and allowing infrastructure to expand at any cost or pace," she said.
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

articles.title_orig: China's space station sets new atomic cooling record
articles.title_zh: China's space station sets new atomic cooling record
articles.content_orig:
Scientists brought thousands of rubidium atoms to less than 10 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero
That is about four times colder than the previous best, set in a German drop tower, and colder than anything reached by Nasa’s Cold Atom Lab on the International Space Station (ISS). The cloud held together for seven seconds, much longer than the two seconds achieved in the drop tower and about one second aboard the ISS.
Nick Bigelow, a physicist at the University of Rochester who has led experiments on Nasa’s lab, called the findings “wonderful results”. He said his own team has since cooled atoms to about 15 trillionths of a degree, in work not yet published, so the Chinese result still comes out on top.

articles.title_orig: Trump blames Democrats for stock market plunge after sweeping midterm victories
articles.title_zh: Trump blames Democrats for stock market plunge after sweeping midterm victories
articles.content_orig:
BEP Research founder Ben Pouladian analyzes the technology stock selloff and concerns surrounding artificial intelligence infrastructure on ‘Making Money.’
President Donald Trump blamed Democrats' sweeping midterm election victories for Thursday's massive stock market sell-off, as Wall Street suffered its sharpest losses since April 2025.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump warned that the market plunge had taken a toll on Americans' retirement savings.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," Trump wrote.
"Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this," he continued. "Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped."
STOCKS PLUNGE AS DEM MIDTERM SWEEP FUELS AI REGULATORY CONCERNS
President Donald Trump blamed Democrats' sweeping midterm election victories for Thursday's sharp stock market sell-off, warning that Americans' retirement savings had taken a hit. (Reuters/Elizabeth Frantz / Reuters)
Trump lashed out at Democrats, placing blame for Thursday's losses squarely on the party's election gains , which included winning control of both the House and Senate.
"Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats," he wrote. "Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE."
U.S. stocks plunged Thursday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 1,833 points, or 3.44%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52%, its worst session since April 2025.
The S&P 500 also declined 4.36%, while the Nasdaq entered correction territory, closing more than 10% below its October record high.
HOW DEMOCRATS’ MIDTERM GAINS COULD RESHAPE THE POLITICAL LANDSCAPE FOR AI
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,833 points, or 3.44%, Thursday as U.S. stocks suffered steep losses following the midterm elections. (Yuki Iwamura/AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The sell-off was driven in part by steep losses in technology and artificial intelligence stocks as investors weighed the potential impact of Democratic election victories on AI regulation and data center development.
Nvidia fell more than 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12%, FOX Business previously reported.
"The obvious catalyst for the sharp selloff is that markets are pricing in the midterm results," eToro market analyst Jakub Rochlitz said.
The market downturn came just one day after stocks rallied following the midterm elections, wiping out the previous session's gains.

President Donald Trump criticized Democrats following a massive Wall Street sell-off that sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1,800 points Thursday. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Beyond the election results, investors have also raised concerns about the enormous borrowing and spending fueling the AI boom, particularly as technology companies expand data centers amid rising energy costs and uncertainty over future returns.
FOX Business' Sophia Compton and Eric Revell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.
The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.
In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.
Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.
In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 9.6%. Electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry , also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology fell 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively, as the regional technology rout deepened.
The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday. He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.
"If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."

articles.title_orig: Blue Origin announces rocket upgrades aimed at lower costs, more performance
articles.title_zh: Blue Origin announces rocket upgrades aimed at lower costs, more performance
articles.content_orig:
KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.
Blue Origin is developing a third stage for New Glenn called GS3 (creatively named Glenn Stage 3) to offer direct injection to geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The third stage fits within an interstage, preserving the full fairing volume for customer payloads.
The stage can fly on both the smaller 7×2 variant (as in seven first stage engines and two second stage engines) of New Glenn as well as the larger 9×4 variant. According to Blue Origin, a GS3-equipped New Glenn 7×2 can carry 8 metric tons directly to geostationary orbit and 10 metric tons to translunar injection. Those figures increase to 14 tons and 20 tons, respectively, for the larger 9×4 variant.
As the rocket’s third stage, it needs to be light, Limp said. For this reason, the third stage is made mostly of composites, which are high-performing and lightweight. But there’s a problem with that.
The stage will be powered by the company’s BE-7 engine, already used by its lunar landers. This engine is optimized for in-space operations and uses liquid hydrogen and oxygen propellants. But hydrogen is the smallest atom and therefore leaky. With composites, thermal cycling and mechanical strain can cause cracking, exacerbating losses of molecular hydrogen.
Limp said the company was not sure a large composite tank, 5.5-meter diameter in this case, could be constructed that would contain hydrogen at high pressures.
The company recently had a breakthrough at Launch Site One in Texas, when it completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test. During the test, the tank was pressurized to 100 percent of the maximum force expected during operation for 2.5 hours. It was even successfully tested at 150 percent of this maximum pressure for 10 minutes.
That gave the company confidence that a GS3 based on composite tanks was a concept that could go forward, and now the company is aiming for a debut in 2028 for a government customer.
“We have one customer signed up for cislunar space in 2028,” Limp said. “We are open for business.”

articles.title_orig: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
articles.title_zh: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
articles.content_orig:
Data centres and AI are already becoming politically fraught topics in Australia. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant )
It's hard to imagine that someone was a bigger loser than the Republican Party in yesterday's US midterm "blue wave".
But somehow, things went even worse for the data centre industry.
When data centres were on the ballot, they overwhelmingly lost. There were about 41 different proposals put to voters in ten states, and all but one are on track for a loss for data centres.
An upset in the Texas governor's race saw Democrat Gina Hinojosa sail to victory. This puts Hinojosa, who has called for a ban on data centre construction, in charge of a state that currently has the biggest pipeline for data centre construction . If the ban is carried out, this will likely put a big dent in national construction.
Less directly but perhaps more consequentially, it's also cemented data centres as a politically toxic issue.
Five per cent of all political ads on TV mentioned data centres, and the majority of them were negative. It was an even bigger proportion in states that have become hot spots for data centre construction — the topic was covered in as many as 14 per cent of all political ads in Wisconsin .
An exit poll of voters conducted by NBC News found that three-quarters of voters oppose the construction of data centres in their community. More than 50 per cent of them said it was a crucial issue or major issue in their vote.
The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. ( ABC News: Bec Symons )
Admittedly, data centres weren't the biggest issue overall. Corruption, cost of living, immigration and the Iran War all rated higher. But to keep things in perspective, data centres were not a political issue just two years ago.
I mean this literally: I couldn't find an exit poll that even asked voters about data centres. Nor can I remember a time that a technology issue was so front and centre for voters. (It feels a bit like a cursed monkey's paw somewhere just put one, shrivelled finger down for those who were hoping more people would pay attention to AI.)
By the end of the 2026 midterm elections, data centres had become a bipartisan issue with candidates from both major parties opposing their construction.
(As always, US President Donald Trump was iconoclastic in his increasingly lonely but still vocal support for data centres and his rebranded "super intelligence".)
There will be a lot of ink spilled on what voters were actually rejecting in this data centre repudiation.
Was this motivated by environmental concerns? NIMBYism? The industry's significant contribution to inflation? Is the opposition to data centres a proxy for opposition to AI — obviously intrinsically intertwined as its physical manifest — or the impact of big tech itself?
More broadly, was this white collar voters experiencing a new type of economic anxiety because they fear their roles could be automated using data centres?
It's obviously some combination of the above, but the proportions will matter a lot.
One group keenly watching this result is Australia's political class.
It's not surprising that people who walk the halls of parliament are political sickos like many of us, but they're also certainly taking note of the data centre issue with an eye to what it means for us, here.
We should heed a note of caution against trying to directly transplant the midterm results to our political environment.
Australia is not America in a lot of ways, including when it comes to data centres. We've definitely seen an explosion in construction and proposals for a new generation of bigger, hungrier data centres , but the scale of our build out pales in comparison to our American friends.
The combined capacity of Australia's existing 163 data centres is about 1.6 gigawatts, according to Data Centres Australia. America has about 30 times that, at around 50 gigawatts of capacity, by one estimate .
Our biggest data centre, AirTrunk's MEL1 in western Melbourne, is ten times smaller than the known capacity of Elon Musk's monstrous Colossus 2 (which was reportedly powered for a while by gas turbines without environmental permits , thanks in part to the laxer rules in the land of the free — another difference between our contexts).
Nor is the opposition to data centres here quite at the level of the American backlash. Recent polling found that 44 per cent of Australians would oppose a data centre built near them — not a great number for the industry, but not quite like the 76 per cent of Americans in exit polls.
Another major difference? Australia has a bipartisan consensus from the two major parties on data centres, but in the opposite direction.
Just last month, the chairs of the parliament's joint inquiry into AI — Labor's Jo Briskey and the Liberal's deputy chair Jonathon Duniam — took the unusual step of sending a letter mid-way through the inquiry's investigation to give an "early indicator" of what they'd found.
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam and Labor MP Jo Briskey are co-chairs the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
It outlined several things that would be required to get the top AI companies doing their "training" here — a goal that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also explicitly stated is an objective of his government.
Translation: Australia wants AI companies to build big data centres here.
Now, the Australian politicians, staffers and those in the data centre industry who I spoke to about the midterms aren't completely terrified by the result.
They're very aware of the existing political stigma around data centres. Many of them expect that this result, even though it's in a different context, will embolden anti-data centre organisers, who are already fresh off a few wins in the last few weeks.
But there is a sense that it's possible to avoid this kind of response if we can thread the needle of attracting AI investment — again, this means building data centres — if we do it on, in their words, "our terms".
This is the motivation behind the government's proposed new rules for data centres that are expected to be released by the end of the year.
There are proposals for data centres in many places across Australia. This artist's impression shows one proposed for near Wagga Wagga, NSW. ( Supplied: CDC Data Centres )
There is one other interesting downstream impact of a cooling data centre industry in the US.
With an American data centre slowdown, the computing crunch on major AI companies who are already fighting amongst themselves for resources will get even worse. This means there's even more pressure to look outside of the US. And guess which country is high up on many of the top AI companies' wish lists?
Australia is in a small group of dream destinations for major AI companies, and our leverage just grew. This could mean we can negotiate more from a tech industry increasingly desperate for a new place to call home: more money, stricter rules, a greater say over how they run — it's all on the table.
That must be an enticing thought for politicians already banking on extract concessions from these companies to piggyback our own AI industry and to jump-start our economy.
But there's probably another question itching at the back of their minds: Is this febrile feeling by the electorate towards data centres a cautionary tale that we can avoid? Or if our government's goal to lure major AI companies down here comes true, is it our political destiny?

articles.title_orig: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR
Published: 14:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EDT, 5 November 2026
Humans have been getting stoned for at least 2,800 years, a new study has revealed.
Scientists from the University of Bern uncovered cannabis seeds in a tomb in Siberia, belonging to high–ranking members of the Scythian society – a horse–riding culture of the Eurasian steppe.
Using radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that the seeds were placed in the grave in the early eighth century BC.
In addition, the scientists found traces of cannabis in human hair collected inside the tomb.
This suggests that the drug had either been inhaled or ingested by one of the tomb's residents.
'The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,' said Dr Gino Caspari, who led the study, published in the journal Science.
Scientists from the University of Bern uncovered cannabis seeds in a tomb in Siberia, belonging to high–ranking members of the Scythian society – a horse–riding culture of the Eurasian steppe
In addition, the scientists found traces of cannabis in human hair collected inside the tomb. This suggests that the drug had either been inhaled or ingested by one of the tomb's residents
While cannabis is one of the most commonly used drugs in the world today, exactly when humans started using it has remained unclear.
Previous studies have shown that cannabis was cultivated in East Asia at least 6,000 years ago, likely initially for its oil–rich seeds.
However, direct evidence of its use has been lacking.
One of the key issues is that plant parts such as flowers, leaves and resins are perishable – meaning they rarely survive.
In their new study, the team explored a tomb in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva.
There, they found about 1,400 cannabis seeds – six of which were in good enough condition to date back around 2,800 years.
'The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,' said Dr Caspari.
However, the seeds alone do no prove that cannabis was consumed by the tomb's residents.
In their new study, the team explored a tomb in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva. There, they found about 1,400 cannabis seeds – six of which were in good enough condition to date back around 2,800 years
The seeds (pictured) alone do no prove that cannabis was consumed by the tomb's residents. Thankfully, the researchers also found human hair in the tomb, which contained 'clear signals' consistent with cannabinol (CBN)
Thankfully, the researchers also found human hair in the tomb, which contained 'clear signals' consistent with cannabinol (CBN).
CBN is produced by the oxidation of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the most important intoxicating compound in cannabis.
In addition, the team detected weak signals that are consistent with THC.
While the discovery within the hair indicates cannabis use, the scientists still don't know how the drug was consumed, or how much of it was taken.
The researchers now hope to analyse the seeds further to understand whether they were specifically selected or cultivated for higher levels of active compounds.
'We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,' says Dr Caspari.
'DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.'
Cannabis is an illegal Class B drug in the UK, meaning possession could result in a five year prison sentence and those who supply the drug face up to 14 years in jail.
However, the drug is widely used for recreational purposes and can make users feel relaxed and happy.
But smoking it can also lead to feelings of panic, anxiety or paranoia.
Scientific studies have shown the drug can alleviate depression, anxiety and stress, but heavy use may worsen depression in the long term by reducing the brain's ability to let go of bad memories.
It can also contribute to mental health problems among people who already have them, or increase users' risk of psychosis or schizophrenia, according to research.
Marijuana can be prescribed for medical uses in more than half of US states, where it is used to combat anxiety, aggression and sleeping problems. Researchers are also looking into whether it could help people with autism,eczema or psoriasis.
Cannabis oil containing the psychoactive chemical THC, which is illegal in the UK, is claimed to have cancer-fighting properties, and one 52 year-old woman from Coventry says she recovered from terminal bowel and stomach cancer by taking the drug.

articles.title_orig: Vulnerability allows attackers to log into some Linux devices sans password
articles.title_zh: Vulnerability allows attackers to log into some Linux devices sans password
articles.content_orig:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday . “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”
When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.
Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.”  Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.
Despite the prerequisites, *sshole —the vulnerability name given by the person who discovered it—likely threatens large numbers of systems. The Docker Hub base image for Alpine has more than 1 billion downloads. Alpine has long been popular in routers, smart TVs, industrial controllers, and other types of embedded devices, many of which can’t be easily updated, if at all. More recently, Alpine has been adopted for use in desktops and servers. Alpine is also used in many container images.
According to security firm Detectify, Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22. Only a fraction meet the conditions necessary for exploitation, but given the ease and speed of testing each one, locating vulnerable devices won’t require much effort or time.
It’s not entirely clear where the vulnerability resides. OpenSSH, which issued an update Thursday, said : “We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside sshd, but it is exploitable via sshd and can be avoided there.” Musl developer Rich Felker, meanwhile, wrote : “It is my position that this is not a bug in musl just an erroneous use by the caller.” Felker went on to say that musl developers have wanted to make changes to the mechanism “for a while now” and planned to do so in an upcoming release. Alpine has also issued an update.
It’s not yet known what other packages may be vulnerable. The person who discovered *sshole said OpenWRT is affected, but by default, that OS uses the Dropbear package, not OpenSSH, for SSH connections (though maintainers provide instructions for installing the latter). The discoverer also names the packages buildroot and yocto as being affected, but that isn’t yet confirmed.
Despite the uncertainty, anyone using a Linux system that uses both musl and OpenSSH should take time to immediately investigate if they’re affected. A good starting point is here . Both Alpine and OpenSSH patches should be installed on all affected systems. There is no known CVE designation for the vulnerability.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's Peña resigns as bank collapse triggers political crisis
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's Peña resigns as bank collapse triggers political crisis
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is facing a criminal investigation and impeachment proceedings following the collapse of a major bank he had business links to.
Peña announced his resignation from office earlier on Thursday after Ueno Bank was shut down in the middle of the night due to a solvency crisis, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money and triggering a scandal.
Paraguay’s Attorney General has opened three criminal cases against Peña and other former officials related to the bank crisis.
The lower chamber of Congress has approved his impeachment, accusing him of “serious and systematic dereliction of duty” in connection with his dealings with the bank. The Senate later announced that it would start an impeachment trial.
Peña said he would present himself in the trial and defend himself: “I will do so with arguments and evidence, with respect for the Constitution and the institutions of the Republic,” he said.
Peña submitted his resignation while lawmakers were debating charges brought against him by 35 opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents. The charges proposed “removing from office” the president, who took power in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Soon after he announced he would resign, Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to trigger impeachment proceedings.
Both chambers of Congress then convened a joint session on whether to accept his resignation, but it was adjourned without a decision after several lawmakers walked out in the middle of the vote.
If lawmakers had accepted his resignation, he would have been given immunity and special protections; if they remove him from power, he won’t.
Lawmakers that oppose the president said Peña is still president and must face justice.
His impeachment trial started in the Senate on Thursday night and is expected to continue Friday.
“This guy, Santiago Peña, needs to be jailed. An arrest warrant must be issued … pretrial detention, straight to jail,” Senator Yolanda Paredes told reporters earlier.
Peña’s party, the right-wing Colorado Party, has a majority in both houses of Congress.
The presidential office insisted that Peña would show up to the trial. A spokesperson dismissed rumors that he had fled the country, saying he remains in the capital without specifying his exact whereabouts.
Peña said earlier that he was resigning to give peace of mind to Paraguayans “who entrusted their savings to our financial system.”
“I have made the decision to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our public institutions in mind,” he said in a message posted on social media.
Peña entered office as one of the youngest presidents in Paraguayan history at the age of 44. He served as Minister of Finance from 2015 to 2017 during the presidency of Horacio Cartes and also served as a director of the Central Bank.
He is one of the staunchest allies of US President Donald Trump’s administration and has aligned with Trump’s political priorities, particularly on immigration and security.
In response to the president’s announced resignation, a US State Department spokesperson said the relationship between both countries remains strong: “We remain committed to the enduring relationship between the American and Paraguayan people and look forward to continuing our close cooperation on shared priorities.”
Paraguay’s president became embroiled in the crisis that erupted after the intervention of Ueno Bank, a private institution to which he has been linked and which, during his administration, received millions in funds from public entities, including the Social Security Institute (IPS), which manages the pensions of most of the country’s workers.
CNN contacted the presidency before Peña’s resignation to ask about the allegations against him.
The Central Bank of Paraguay found that Ueno Bank’s solvency ratio — with 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people — had fallen below 50% of the required minimum, “as a result of adjustments made to its financial statements during the regularization process.”
As a result of the resolution or dissolution proceedings, the savings of millions of customers were frozen at the financial institution, which is also known for sponsoring local soccer teams and Paraguay’s national team.
Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández ordered the opening of three cases to investigate “the supervision and resolution of Ueno Bank SA, the placement of public funds in said entity and the actions of authorities from different State institutions.”
Paraguay was shaken by Tuesday’s intervention of Ueno, an institution that, according to authorities, violated limits on loans to related companies.
Paraguay’s Central Bank said Thursday night it would start processing guarantee payments to certain Ueno customers in stages.
Peña announced his resignation after two days of long lines at banks, anxiety and street protests.
The country has been trying to position itself as a regional financial hub by capitalizing on the investment-grade status it attained in recent years, after receiving approval from two of the world’s leading rating agencies.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres, Ivonne Valdés Garay and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Phones 'explode' on Wall Street as 'steamroller' shows up for the AI trade
articles.title_zh: Phones 'explode' on Wall Street as 'steamroller' shows up for the AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Saqib Iqbal Ahmed, Anirban Sen, Nupur Anand and Laura Matthews
NEW YORK, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Phones rang off the hook on Wall Street on Thursday as fear-stricken investors sought guidance from the rapid unraveling of the AI trade.
Spooked retail investors and hedge funds alike dumped stocks, Wall Street's fear gauge spiked ‌and traders rushed to hedge as markets went into a tailspin.
"The steamroller showed up today," said Jim Carroll, senior wealth adviser and portfolio manager at Ballast Rock ‌Private Wealth in Charleston, South Carolina.
The Nasdaq 100 index fell 6.4%, erasing $2.5 trillion in market value on investor fears that the Democratic Party's sweeping midterm victory could stall AI infrastructure expansion, adding more uncertainty to a trade ​that has been on shaky ground for the last several weeks.
"Our phones are exploding with asks for color," John Flood, partner and managing director in the global banking and markets division at Goldman Sachs, said in a note.
A person at another large Wall Street bank said investors were increasingly anxious about the unfolding situation.
The selloff sparked hefty hedging in the equity options market as investors braced for further weakness. Wall Street's most closely watched gauge of anxiety, the Cboe Volatility Index, logged its biggest intraday jump in more than 18 months.
Analysts said much of the selling reflected an unwind of the ‌previous session's rally and of the crowded AI trade that has ⁠driven markets for months.
"There was massive de-risking into midterms and traders were surprised by yesterday's move and got sucked back in," Flood said, adding that hedge funds were selling pockets of the market, like hyperscalers, that they bought the previous day.
Options activity was a mix of traders looking for ⁠fresh protection in semiconductors and AI names alongside those taking profits on existing hedges, said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivative strategy at Susquehanna Financial.
The VIX, an options-based indicator that reflects demand for protection against drops in the stock market, jumped 11.75 points to an eight-month high of 28.36, a day after markets rallied following Democrats' victory.
The index closed at 28.18, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% as investors ​fretted ​that a changing of the guard in Washington might slow the pace of AI infrastructure development.
The selloff was in ​sharp contrast to the upbeat market reaction the day before, when ‌investors largely brushed aside the perceived threat to the AI trade from the election results.
"Yesterday there was the perception that no one needed protection and now it's 'Oh my god, we need it'," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.
Analysts attributed some of the decline to investors looking to get ahead of anticipated selling from strategies that react to market volatility.
Leveraged and inverse exchange-traded funds, along with some systematic strategies, typically rebalance near the market close. They also tend to respond as markets grow more volatile, which can amplify market moves.
Leveraged ETFs were expected to sell about $47 billion of stocks into the close as they rebalance, according to an intraday note from Nomura. That would make it the second-largest amount in Nomura's data going back to ‌July 2006, with most of it coming from tech and AI-focused funds.
HEDGE FUND, RETAIL REACTION
Hedge funds were ​also feeling the pain.
According to a Goldman Sachs prime brokerage report sent to clients on November 5, large ​multi-strategy hedge funds were down "significantly" due to outsized exposure to large AI stocks. Technology, ​media and telecommunications-focused funds were down 2.6% from a year ago, Goldman said.
Much now depends on whether investors' attitude toward the AI trade undergoes ‌a lasting change, analysts said.
"If the re-evaluation of the AI investment theme ​is secular and not just a trading type ​of rebalance, that's problematic," said Sosnick.
Retail selling added to market pressure. About one hour before the close, they were on track for their largest day of selling across single stocks since the COVID-related crash, said Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, in an intraday note.
"On a typical sell-off, retail buy the dip. Today, that bid ​has effectively disappeared from individual names," Patel said.
In the options market, ‌the stock market drop boosted demand for hedges, with put premiums — the prices investors pay to buy contracts that protect against a market drop — running at ​about two times what is typical across index products, according to options analytics service Mercury Alerts.
(Reporting by Saqib Iqbal Ahmed; Additional reporting by Laura Matthews, Anirban Sen, ​Nupur Anand, Suzanne McGee; editing by Megan Davies, Kirsten Donovan, Nia Williams and David Gaffen)

articles.title_orig: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.title_zh: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.content_orig:
Navy and Marine Corps leaders have recently come to the agreement that the Corps needs 40 amphibious ships to meet its goal of keeping three Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) deployed at the same time. However, at the moment, the Navy has only 31 of these vessels, a minimum mandated by Congress, and now an effort is underway to convince lawmakers to increase the fleet.
MEUs, made up of about 2,200 Marines, are typically embarked on Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), which usually consist of an assault ship, two transport docks or dock landing ships. Support vessels, surface combatants and in some cases a nuclear fast attack submarine can make up the larger Expeditionary Strike Group.
Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Eric Smith’s top priority is meeting what is called the 3.0 ARG/MEU presence, said Shon Brodie, director of Maritime Expeditionary Warfare at the Corps’ Combat Development and Integration (CD&I) Directorate tasked with modernizing the Marines.
Smith “believes that the best thing that we as a service can do for the nation is provide the highly trained Marine Expeditionary Units, one from the East Coast, one from the West Coast, and that one in Japan, persistently,” Brodie told a small group of reporters, including from TWZ , on Wednesday.
To ensure that happens, Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO) Adm. James W. Kilby and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps (ACMC) Gen. Bradford J. Gering “have worked really close together to try to understand the number of ships it would require to achieve 3.0 based on current readiness,” Brodie noted.
“The two analytical arms of both services have come to the conclusion that it takes 40 ships. That’s 13 big decks and 27 LPDs,” the Maritime Expeditionary Warfare director explained.
Big decks are the Navy’s Wasp class (LHD) and America class (LHA) amphibious assault ships. Their embarked Aviation Combat Elements (ACEs) can include F-35B Joint Strike Fighters , MV-22 tiltrotor aircraft , UH-1 , AH-1 and CH-53 helicopters , as well as Navy Seahawk helicopters . The LPDs are smaller [ Amphibious Transport Dock ships ], which also embark MV-22s and helicopters.
The capabilities of MEUs have grown over the past decade, allowing them, in limited cases, to take on tasks that once required an aircraft carrier strike group. MV-22 tiltrotors, and, more recently, F-35Bs, which can be embarked in large numbers in the so-called “Lightning carrier” configuration, have boosted the utility of these fighting units.
The amphibious ship requirements, which had been in discussion for a while, were finally hammered out over the past few months by the new Amphibious Force Readiness Board (AFRB), stated Brodie. The AFRB is a joint Navy-Marine Corps effort created to better track the readiness of the amphibious fleet , which has been a huge issue as we have frequently noted .
“Right now, I have 31 amphibious warfare ships,” stated Brodie. The biggest need at the moment, he added, is for additional amphibious assault ships.
The law calls for the service to have 10, but currently it has only nine. That’s because the USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD-6) was sent to the scrapyard in 2021 after being ravaged by a fire in 2020 .
Brodie said the Marines want to increase the number of mandated amphibious assault ships from 10 to 13.
“When I have a problem generating this force, it really revolves around the big deck,” he stated.
The call for a fleet of 40 amphibious ships, and especially 13 big decks, is a sharp departure from the guidance former Commandant Gen. David Berger introduced in 2019 that led to his Force Design 2030 plan . In these documents, Berger called for fewer amphibious assault ships and more smaller vessels . Berger was concerned about the growing array of threats to these large, slow-moving vessels from anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, and that was before one-way attack drones became such ubiquitous weapons of war. This strategy was seen as better suited for fighting in the Pacific in a modern context, not large scale beach landings of the past.
He also wanted to return the Corps to its naval roots ; small, dispersed stand-in forces working inside an adversary’s weapons engagement zone after two decades of ground pounding in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Given how much of a sea-change this new plan represents, reaching a 40 amphibious ship fleet that includes 13 big decks is no small task.
“I’ve got a sheet sitting right here in front of me that tells me how we get there,” Brodie added. “You can’t get there tomorrow, right? The only way for me to realistically increase that inventory is for me to build new ships and do a service-life extension on some of the selective ships that I currently have in the inventory.”
Brodie said that Kilby and Gering are going to approach Congress later this month to convey the need for more ships.
There is no set timeline to reach the 40-ship goal, the Marines told TWZ .
“We will have to await future congressional funding for these,” Lt. Col. Eric D. Flanagan, a USMC spokesman, told us, adding that there is a multi-ship procurement contract underway for several amphibious vessels. He was referring to HII being awarded a $9.6 billion multi-ship procurement contract in 2024 for the construction of three San Antonio class amphibious ships and a contract modification for the next America class large-deck amphibious ship.
“This combined procurement — the first of its kind for amphibious ships — begins the journey for the construction of LPDs 33, 34, 35 and LHA 10 for the U.S. Navy,” HII stated at the time .
The request for additional shipbuilding funds will likely face far stiffer headwinds now that the Democrats have won control of both the Senate and the House.
While the Trump administration continues to pursue a roughly $1.5 trillion defense budget for Fiscal Year 2027, which includes some $350 billion that would come from outside normal defense spending streams via the reconciliation process , a letter leaked yesterday from a top Democrat offers a glimpse into the challenges the new amphibious ship plan may face.
The letter from Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington state Democrat who is in line to become chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, makes clear that many programs and policy issues, as well as defense spending writ large, are set to be put under the microscope when the Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote in his ‘dear colleagues’ letter.
All of this comes at a time when the Navy has been struggling to meet operational demands for surface combatants with its existing fleet. This has been further exacerbated by shakeups in separate plans to acquire new frigates and larger uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), as well as rising costs associated with its workhorse Arleigh Burke class destroyers .
On top of everything, conflicts in the Middle East have taken a toll on the Navy, incurring costs that need to be paid for.
In August, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle estimated as a result of the Operation Epic Fury fight against Iran, the Navy needed between $6 billion and $8 billion more than what was budgeted for in the 2026 fiscal year “to be whole and solvent for [Fiscal Year] 26,” Navy Times reported .
Overall, the U.S. military “has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July,” according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters last month .
In addition to not having enough ships to fulfill the mission, there is a big problem keeping the existing ones available. The Navy’s amphibious ship fleet had just a 47% combat surge readiness rate as of April, according to Kilby’s Fiscal Year 2027 budget request statement . As we have pointed out pr

articles.title_orig: Retail traders dump $265 million in stocks in biggest selling day since 2020
articles.title_zh: Retail traders dump $265 million in stocks in biggest selling day since 2020
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Retail investors dumped US stocks on Thursday at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $265 million in individual US stocks on Thursday, according to Vanda Research, the biggest single-day net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.2%, putting the index on track to close in a correction.
Retail selling marks something of a departure from a tendency by individual investors in recent years to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued to purchase leveraged exchange-traded funds such as ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Vanda added that net selling was a third higher earlier Thursday afternoon before late "late-session" retail buyers stepped in
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.

articles.title_orig: Canada's federal budget includes billions for sovereignty and tackling homelessness
articles.title_zh: Canada's federal budget includes billions for sovereignty and tackling homelessness
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living.
"That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday.
"It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish."
The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing.
The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War.
Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; £27bn), with no path to balance.
Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact.
The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year.
But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian.
And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment.
Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget.
One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness.
This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment.
Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime.
The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year.
Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on  cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues.
There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs.
The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver.
And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive.
After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly.
This includes a cap on international students and temporary foreign workers, which have been relied on by companies to ease labour shortages.
The Carney government has previously said it will keep its permanent resident admission target to 380,000 people annually until 2028.
Meanwhile, it will gradually reduce its temporary resident arrivals to 370,000.
There has been pressure on Carney to increase some of those numbers. A report from the Royal Bank of Canada in September warned that "without immigration, the country's population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century".
On the other hand, the Conservative opposition has called on the government to further lower its targets.
In the new budget, Carney has opted to keep immigration levels flat.
A big focus of the Carney government has been reducing Canada's reliance on the US as a trade partner, while also helping cushion the blow from Trump's tariffs on its key sectors.
Last year, it promised millions in backing for businesses working to develop new export markets. It also lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate in a bid to stop businesses from moving to the US to escape tariff pains.
This budget builds on that, including plans to support specific sectors hit by US tariffs like steel and forestry.
The new funding was welcome by Canada's forestry sector, with the BC Council of Forest Industries saying in a statement that the support "comes at a critical time for workers".
Since March 2025, the Carney government has set aside nearly C$44bn in support for workers and businesses hit by US tariffs, the budget notes.
The budget states that "diversification will take time, given the scale and depth of Canada's economic relationship with the United States. But the shift is underway".
Sovereignty is a big theme in Carney's second budget, which proposes funding different measures to strengthen Canadian identity - whether it be through the arts or in space.
Canada is the only G7 country that does not have the capability to launch its own rockets. A line item in the budget looks to change that, with C$2.7bn earmarked to developing Canadian space technology and launch infrastructure.
On arts and culture, Carney is promising a tax exemption on income that is made through "original and creative artistic works".
The budget also sets aside C$32.2m over four years to establish a free national digital library for Canadians. It will launch with at least 200 titles with plans to expand in coming years.
Carney had previously pledged to significantly boost defence spending to meet the Nato target of 5% of annual GDP by 2035.
This year's budget provides some insight into where that money is being spent.
That includes a marketplace, launched earlier this year, to sell Canadian-made drones. It will get a cash injection of C$2.3bn over five years.
More funding will also go into support for Operation Reassurance, Canada's largest overseas deployment mission to deter Russian aggression in eastern Europe.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine knocks out 15 Russian oil refineries, causing $23.2 billion in damage: officials
articles.title_zh: Ukraine knocks out 15 Russian oil refineries, causing $23.2 billion in damage: officials
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv’s airstrikes have knocked 15 of Russia’s 38 major oil refineries out of operation — causing more than $23.2 billion in economic damage, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said Thursday.
Just 12 refineries are running at reduced capacity following the precision strikes, which wiped out nearly all of Moscow’s oil sector income from 2025, the HUR estimated.
The agency specifically cited five facilities that were hit as of September, including the massive  Ryazan Oil Refining Company, with those refineries accounting for 33% of Russia’s total volumes.
The strikes have effectively cut Russia’s processing volumes by 55.4% compared to the beginning of the year, Kyiv added.
The attacks have served as a major headache for Moscow, which relies on its oil to fund its ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
The refinery attacks have also led to a gas shortage in various Russian regions, including the annexed Crimea, with more citizens feeling the pain in their wallets over the ongoing war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has reiterated that he would be open to stopping the repeated strikes on Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin halts its attacks on Kyiv’s energy infrastructure.
Moscow has refused to comply , with Zelensky telling world leaders on Thursday that Russian suicide drones continue to hit his country’s critical infrastructure.
“Russians are using Shahed drones and missiles to hit even the energy equipment that our nuclear power plants depend on,” Zelensky said in his address at the Ibero-American Summit. “Every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by Russian attacks.”
Ukraine and Russia continue to trade attacks, with Moscow bombing a postal logistics hub of Nova Poshta, Ukraine’s largest private delivery company, according to the Kremlin.
The Russians also hit a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk and a cargo ship in the Black Sea, the Kremlin said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone strikes set off fires in an industrial zone in the city of Ryazan, about 125 miles southeast of Moscow.

articles.title_zh: Memory Stocks Are Tanking. Should You Buy the Dip?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

articles.title_orig: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.title_zh: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in AI development.
Following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI, shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index closed down by more than 5.5% to lose an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
Democrats in races across the US  campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
Live: What can Democrats do with control of Congress? We answer your US midterms questions
Food, fuel and taxes â can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .

articles.title_orig: Neocloud IREN says $4 billion in annualized revenue being delayed due to customer request
articles.title_zh: Neocloud IREN says $4 billion in annualized revenue being delayed due to customer request
articles.content_orig:
Following a 26% post-election plunge in its stock price, neocloud IREN said in its earnings report on Thursday that over $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to land in 2026 has been pushed out to at least January.
IREN said the move, which could extend payment to February, is due to "a customer-requested change and supplier timing."
On the company's earnings call, IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts said Microsoft is the customer.
"They made a request to reconfigure and upgrade some of the network infrastructure and the purpose of that was really to enable the 200 megawatts of capacity to service these latest-generation frontier models," Roberts said.
Shares of IREN rose in extended trading, but that comes after a 55% drop over the past month.
The company said revenue climbed 66% from the prior quarter to $228 million, beating the $221 million average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AI Cloud revenue more than doubled to $200 million. IREN gets the rest of its revenue from bitcoin mining, which was its primary business before the company pivoted to AI.
IREN's net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million the prior period. Year-ago figures weren't included in the earnings release.
The company is being closely watched by investors as the AI trade shows signs of unwinding , particularly following the Democratic sweep in Tuesday's midterm elections. Concerns are mounting that cash-burning companies reliant on debt are going to have a hard time meeting their obligations as interest rates rise and lenders back out of the market. The Nasdaq had its worst day on Thursday since April 2025.
"Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the call.
CoreWeave , which is set to report earnings on Tuesday, has plunged 60% in the past month. Nebius , which reports next Thursday, is down 48% over that stretch.
IREN said revenue backlog increased 22% from the prior period to $20.3 billion, with "approximately two-thirds with investment-grade counterparties." The $4 billion ARR target is fully contracted and funded, the company said.
"There is a disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level," Roberts told CNBC's Seema Mody.
Still, Iren said it planed to shell out $15 billion in capital expenditures the rest of this fiscal year, including $9 billion in cash and committed financing, and $6 billion in "target" financing, which is "subject to market conditions."
The neocloud said that prices for its compute continue to rise and that it expanded an existing contract with a leading frontier AI lab. It said it has contracts with Nvidia , Microsoft and 13 other customers.
Roberts said that some data center construction in the coming year would be backed by Nvidia and Microsoft, but about a third would be to companies that are willing to offer large prepayments for the capacity.
"We just had a customer agree to fund 90% of the GPU capex," Roberts said, referring to graphics processing units.
IREN said that community opposition can be addressed by tapping local suppliers, using water efficiently and creating jobs.
"I think whether it's Texas, whether it's Australia, whether it's Spain, everywhere, all we're seeing is people wanting to ensure that data centers pay their own way and do the right thing, and it it feels completely reasonable," Roberts said.
IREN said it deliberately hadn't yet bought all of the GPUs it needs for next year to reduce risk.
—CNBC's Isabel O'Brien contributed to this report.
