articles.title_orig: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
articles.title_zh: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
articles.content_orig:
Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.
Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.
The new MDR-3R (note the slightly different name) headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions.
New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector.
“The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize,” Sony’s announcement says.
For better or worse, the new headphones also use “the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original,” per Sony. Audiophiles will prefer something more advanced, perhaps with additional acoustic features. A review of the new headphones from Gizmodo says that the MDR-3R headphones “hold their own,” have “bright and clear” mids and highs, and good stereo separation. However, we don’t expect strong bass.
Unlike their predecessor, the MDR-3R has an in-line remote control and an integrated microphone. Without noise-canceling, though, the microphone isn’t ideal for calls in noisy environments.
But nostalgic gear isn’t about having top-of-the-line capabilities; it’s about showing off your love of old-school tech while enjoying familiar technologies that have reliably served their functions for years.
The MDR-3R may also capitalize on surging renewed interest in wired headphones and even physical media and Walkmans. Today’s Walkmans aren’t cassette players, of course, but are Android-powered , touchscreen media players.
The headphones are available for $60.

articles.title_orig: More than a dozen flights in Europe receive bomb threats that an official calls 'malicious' hoaxes
articles.title_zh: More than a dozen flights in Europe receive bomb threats that an official calls 'malicious' hoaxes
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — A wave of bomb threats against passenger airliners caused chaos in the skies and airports of Europe on Thursday, the latest of such incidents this week that have prompted emergency landings and security sweeps on runways.
No explosives have so far been found, and it is not clear who or what is behind the security threats made against at least 14 airliners. But the threats have caused disruption to Europe’s airspace and some of its busiest airports.
The threats against two flights that landed in Rome came by email that cited opposition to “your feminist regime,” the airport confirmed to NBC News. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is a woman who has conservative views.
One of the first reports involved Aer Lingus Flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome, which changed course near Paris and diverted to a French air force base, the airline said. There, all 151 passengers and six crewmembers were evacuated while a bomb squad inspected the aircraft, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said in a statement.
From there, reports of threats in the skies over Europe arrived at a dizzying pace, triggering searches by cabin crews and then again by airport security crews on the ground.
Security operations were launched at airports in Prague; Copenhagen, Denmark; and Warsaw, Poland, where passengers saw the military and police sniffer dogs patrolling the tarmac.
“It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked,” Apostolos Tzitzikostas, the European commissioner for sustainable transport and tourism, said at a news conference in Brussels.
British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander appealed for calm, telling Sky News, “We have established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats, and that’s what these threats have been.”
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport “following anonymous reports of a suspected bomb threat,” said a spokesperson for the city’s airport authority. Bomb disposal experts found nothing.
“Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when other airlines in Europe have also faced hoax bomb threats,” a Finnair spokesperson, Stiina Tuunanen, said in an email. “Threats are almost always unfounded.”
That was also the case for another Finnair flight from Helsinki to Vienna, whose threat was found to be baseless after it landed safely in the Austrian capital.
LOT Polish Airlines said two of its aircraft from Warsaw were targeted, one flying to Brussels and the other to Paris.
Back on the ground in Warsaw, Polish resident Matthew Bojarsky, 28, was about to fly to Paris for a romantic trip with his American girlfriend, but he saw police, military and sniffer dogs on the tarmac, he told NBC News. Passengers were told that “safety protocols” meant their flight, LOT LO331, had to be aborted and moved to a later time.
Elsewhere, three Ryanair flights were interrupted as they headed to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. Two flights, from Copenhagen and Milan, landed at their destination, while a third, from London, was diverted to the city of Plovdiv, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said in an email.
Ryanair did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Romania’s intelligence agency said a KLM flight to Tel Aviv with a layover in Bucharest had received a bomb threat.
And Spanish police said three emailed threats came in within 20 minutes involving two Air Europa departures from Madrid to Paris and four inbound Iberia flights from Rome and Milan. Several aircraft were halted or returned to their stands in Madrid, and passengers disembarked as the aircraft were inspected.
In the Czech Republic, meanwhile, police said they had received threats about improvised explosive devices being placed on four planes heading to the country’s capital, Prague.
In this instance, it appeared that at least some of the threats were sent by email, so “clearly there must be a process whereby airlines distinguish more credible threats from obvious hoaxes,” said Peter Neumann, a professor of security studies at Kings College London.
Thursday’s incidents follow days of airline bomb threats that have forced multiple flights to divert and an airport in Poland to close briefly. No explosive devices were found in the earlier incidents, according to authorities in various countries.
On Tuesday, a security operation was also launched at the Greek island port ⁠of Syros after a bomb threat ​to an Israel-bound cruise ship. Authorities said an unknown person claimed an explosive device had been attached to ⁠the hull of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris, which was due to sail ⁠to Haifa.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents, and there were no claims of responsibility.
Alexander Smith is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.title_zh: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

articles.title_orig: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.title_zh: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.content_orig:
Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing.
The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.
The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students. If they don’t want any AI, they can leave it all off. Essentially, Google is giving schools that want to completely block AI the ability to go all the way, even removing search from student accounts.
A Google spokesperson tells Ars that the company has not made any changes to the new policy it announced this week. However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do. There are still reasons to dislike Google’s approach, but here’s how the company explains the process for schools:
As things currently stand, schools can block the Gemini app, but the AI tools in search (AI Overviews and AI Mode) are still present and offer many of the same intellectual shortcuts. When schools choose which AI features to use under this new system, search will be one of the options. Schools can leave search off if they want, but opting in will require them to choose the standard AI features or the new Guided Learning version, which won’t give away answers as readily (or so Google claims).
Schools are gaining the ability to block Google’s AI tools, even those in search, while keeping other Google apps. Notably, the company’s new approach to “responsible AI for learning” does not include the ability to use search without AI. So schools get more control, even if they don’t get the AI-free search everyone seems to want.
Many will argue that Google should let schools access web search without chatbots. However, that’s just not something Google wants to support at any level because it sees AI as the future of search. While other search engines have settings to turn off AI tools, Google steadfastly refuses to create such a toggle (and those no-AI tricks you rely on may not work forever). Ultimately, this is the core problem not just for education customers, but for everyone who wants to limit their exposure to AI while using Google.
This clarification does not change the calculus for educators who want to allow students to search the Internet without AI tools. Google won’t offer that, and switching to another provider is easier said than done. Google still has by far the most expansive index of the Internet, leaving alternatives with numerous gaps. That may change in the near future, though. As a result of Google’s loss in the DOJ’s search antitrust case , it will have to provide competitors limited access to its index of the web. This could give other provides a chance to improve and offer a more viable alternative to Google.

articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk spent a fortune on the doomed GOP midterms, but his losses are still piling up days later as SpaceX and Tesla shares tank.
The rout in both Tesla and SpaceX continued for a second day on Thursday, with both stocks tumbling in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept the Democrats back into power in Congress and across the US.
By Thursday's closing bell, Tesla had dropped 14% in two days, while SpaceX lost about 13%.
Thoughts that Democrats might be bullish for EVs, and therefore Tesla, were quickly overshadowed by other concerns about what the election outcome could mean for Musk's business empire.
Thoughts have quickly turned to the fate of potential SpaceX-Tesla merger , a prospect that's been a major bull catalyst for investors this year.
"I think that this merger is now at risk, and I think that it will be hard to complete with so much volatility and with high interest rates and and the lack of investment," Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told Business Insider.
Democrats could place much greater regulatory scrutiny on any merger talks, or even force Musk himself to come before Congress in light of reports that he recently throttled Starlink service to Ukraine amid its war with Russia.
Gerber, a former Tesla bull, has emerged as an outspoken Musk critic , though he maintains a more bullish stance on SpaceX, a company his firm holds a position in through a previous stake in X.
He added that for Musk, who shifted his firms' headquarters to Texas, the outlook now appears much more fraught as the state ushers in a Democratic governor.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Gordon Johnson, CEO of market research firm GLJ Research agreed that Tesla-SpaceX merger could be in jeopardy following the midterms.
"The problem is timing and scrutiny," he stated. "The plan was to announce in the first half of 2027 and close while Trump is still in office. Now any merger vote plays out while Democrats hold subpoena power over the Starshield/Ukraine throttling, DOGE, and SpaceX's related-party financing."
SpaceX stock is also being caught in the frenzied selling that has hammered data center operators and AI infrastructure names on Thursday. The iShares Semiconductor ETF was heading for its worst day since 2020, and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 6% into a formal correction during the session.
The fear is that Democrats could tighten oversight and regulation of data centers. For SpaceX, this would be a blow, as the company's AI ambitions are a major part of its growth thesis. Meanwhile, the blue wave swept states that are at the epicenter of the AI data center boom, particularly Texas and Georgia. Texas alone is expected to account for up to 30% of data center development through 2030.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Below $200. What History Suggests Is the Floor.
articles.content_orig:
It has been a challenging month for big tech stocks , including the biggest, Nvidia ( NVDA -9.26% ) .
The world's most valuable company has seen its stock price plummet about 15% since Oct. 6, down to $203 per share as of Nov. 4.
With the artificial intelligence (AI) chip maker set to release third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17, is Nvidia stock a buy at a discount?
Image source: Getty Images.
Nvidia is the leading provider of graphics processing unit (GPU) chips for data centers and AI computing with a market share of about 75% to 80%.
But Nvidia stock , which has averaged a 65% annualized return over the past three years, has sputtered over the past year. It is up just 9% year to date and over the last 12 months it is up just 2%, trading at $203 per share.
Its struggles mainly stem from continuing concerns over capital expenditures on AI infrastructure by hyperscalers. Will it deliver ROI, or will it just be a drain on earnings and cash flows?
Nvidia is one of the major beneficiaries of that spending, so if these hyperscalers scale back for any reason, might the pullback hurt Nvidia?
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/05/26
Also, Nvidia stock tends to move in tandem with the broader tech sector, which has been trending lower over the past month over these concerns, among others, like high valuations.
But there are other reasons for Nvidia's sluggishness. Some analysts and investors have expressed concern over its so-called "circular financing," with Nvidia investing in companies to have them become its customers.
In addition, its market share, though still high, has dropped from a high of 87% in 2024. Some are also worried that its share could erode further with more competitors, including hyperscalers themselves, making their own chips.
Nvidia has also projected its gross margin to decrease in Q3 to 71% to 72%, down from 75% in Q2. This is due to price increases for its memory components. But the company expects a rebound in fiscal 2028.
Furthermore, the Nov. 3 election brought Democratic control of the House and Senate, and that brings greater uncertainties around the landscape for AI and data center development.
So, with Nvidia's Q3 earnings just two weeks away on Nov. 17, is Nvidia stock a buy?
The fact remains, Nvidia continues to generate huge revenue. In the last quarter, revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion while AI data center revenue surged 117% to $89 billion. Revenue is anticipated to hit $108 billion in Q3, which would be up 131% from $46.7 billion in Q3 the previous year.
Further, spending on AI by the five hyperscalers is expected to increase to $1.3 trillion in 2027, up from $800 billion in 2026. This is due to a backlog for cloud computing that is over $2 trillion.
The recent sell-off has brought Nvidia stock down, and it's trading at just 25 times earnings and 13 times forward earnings. Any opportunity to get shares of Nvidia at its current low valuation is hard to pass up.

articles.title_orig: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of thousands of striking workers have walked off their jobs across France and marched against the rising cost of living in a renewed challenge to President Emmanuel Macron, following weeks of student-led demonstrations.
The rallies on Thursday were largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities, including Paris and Lyon, with police firing tear gas.
France’s Interior Ministry said 575,000 people participated in the protests nationwide, while the CGT union, one of the organisers, said 1.6 million had taken part.
At least 448 people were arrested and 53 police officers were injured, the ministry said.
The strikers are demanding a higher minimum wage, raises for all workers, changes to the tax system and better conditions in schools.
“The question is not whether workers will win,” Sophie Binet, the CGT’s leader, told the crowd in Paris, but “how much we’re going to win”.
France has seen regular protests since September, when students began demonstrating against poor conditions in public schools. Their movement has since merged with broader anger over living costs and inequality, which erupted into the country’s worst rioting in years on October 17.
Thursday’s one-day strike was called by unions representing teachers, rail workers, hospital staff and postal employees, and some energy workers joined them. The protest action came five months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with the far right leading in the opinion polls.
The Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe closed for the day, though transport was largely unaffected. About 16 percent of teachers were on strike, according to the Ministry of National Education.
In Paris, the mood was initially festive. A diverse crowd sang the national anthem, “La Marseillaise”, as carnival-style floats rolled through the streets after the main march set off in the afternoon from the Place de la Republique.
Marches in Lyon, Marseille, Nantes and other cities had begun that morning.
In the capital, Jack Eisner, a student at Sciences Po, told Al Jazeera that people are protesting because they feel their “future is at stake”.
“Whether it’s the environmental crisis, whether it’s war, it’s just getting harder and harder to find a job and an education,” he said. “I think a lot of younger people feel the same way and a lot of older people too with the rising prices of goods and fuel.”
About two hours into the march, some protesters at the front clashed with the police, who fired tear gas. The police said hooded individuals had vandalised property and that officers moved immediately to isolate them.
More scuffles broke out as the march wound down, and the authorities put out at least one small fire nearby.
Several high schools in the Paris area were damaged, and one in the city centre was set on fire, regional authorities said.
In Lyon, riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters, some dressed in black with their faces covered, who shouted anti-police slogans. The Interior Ministry said officers there had faced several hundred so-called “black bloc” protesters, and that at least one vehicle was set on fire.
The violence had been contained, the ministry said, though tensions remained high.
At a protest in the northern city of Lille, Hugo, a history student, told Al Jazeera that he was angry about the social situation in France.
“The workers are angry that wages are too low, life is getting more and more expensive and in the universities and high schools, we can feel the lack of public services. So, there is a common anger in the country, and that’s why I am here today. I’m angry about this social situation,” he said.
“There is money in the society, but it’s in the hands of a small group of people, and we have to fight to change the situation,” he added.
In Marseille, Lea, a 31-year-old social worker who did not give her last name, told the AFP news agency that she was tired of counting every euro. “My basket of 20 items has become too expensive,” she said.
“We want cheaper groceries, cheaper petrol.” Still, she said, the movement had given her hope: “It’s been a long time since we’ve seen anything like this.”
Jean-Marc Morel, 60, said he sensed the protests gaining momentum. “There are a lot of us here, and it’s joyful, it’s diverse,” he said. “We’ve got all kinds of professions, old people, young people.”
Several high-profile politicians attended Thursday’s marches, including presidential candidates Jean-Luc Melenchon and Raphael Glucksmann.
Ahead of the protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had promised “an extremely firm response” to any violence, and 70,000 officers were deployed nationwide.
The deployment came after the government faced criticism over its handling of the unrest, with the riots on October 17 leaving damaged shops and public buildings across the country. Allegations of police brutality have also prompted internal investigations, with several teenage protesters seriously wounded in clashes.
French authorities have since imposed curfews, banned large gatherings and required marchers to take routes away from major boulevards, measures the unions have denounced.
“The government tried to block the demonstrations. The demonstrations are bigger than ever,” said Binet, the head of the CGT union.
The strike adds pressure on Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who is scheduled to meet labour unions and employer groups on Monday to discuss wages and living costs.
Polls suggest that Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader, is the front-runner to succeed Macron in April, and that she could face Melenchon in a runoff.
The unrest in France is part of a broader wave of discontent across Europe, with young people in Germany, Spain, Greece and Italy staging similar protests in recent weeks, and demonstrations against falling living standards in Portugal and elsewhere.

SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) has quickly established itself as one of the most exciting stocks in the market. Given the company's growth, I think the stock could generate around $2 trillion in revenue by 2030 and end 2029 with a stock price of $570.
Here's how it would get there.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
SpaceX is focused on the future, and it is pursuing some promising new markets, including orbital data centers, asteroid mining, and Earth-to-Earth cargo transport using suborbital rockets. The road to success in these areas will come down to the company being able to reliably recapture and reuse both stages of its Starship rockets after each launch. If it can pull off this feat, that will set the stage for it to pursue these loftier goals and accelerate its launch cadence.
The company's goal is for the Starship rocket -- a much larger platform than its current Falcon rockets -- to begin flying weekly in the first half of next year, and potentially twice a week starting in the second half of the year. If SpaceX can quickly recover, refurbish, and fully reuse its Starship rockets, it will be able to greatly increase the mass of the payloads it can carry and its number of revenue-generating launches, drastically altering space economics and leading to strong revenue growth in the coming years.
SpaceX is also eyeing disruption of some current industries, like the U.S. mobile phone market. The Starlink satellite broadband business will continue to be a nice revenue driver in the coming years as SpaceX continues to add new commercial, enterprise, and government customers. However, building out a full terrestrial cellphone network would likely take four to six years, so this is more of a medium-term opportunity.
Another growth driver will be AI coding, thanks to SpaceX's recent acquisition of Cursor. Cursor is essentially a workflow interface that can use both its own and third-party AI models to help users write, edit, debug, and review code. Morgan Stanley projects that as a part of SpaceX, Cursor's annual recurring revenue (ARR) will climb from $8 billion at the end of 2026 to roughly $33 billion by the end of 2030.
SpaceX's biggest growth opportunity, however, is likely to come from artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure . The company is poised to become the largest neocloud on the planet, and has set some extremely aggressive goals for itself.
The company will end this year with up to 3 gigawatts of compute capacity, and plans to add around 10 gigawatts more in 2027. Meanwhile, CEO Elon Musk has said his moonshot goal is to bring on 20 gigawatts of additional capacity next year.
SpaceX is currently getting great rates on the compute power it's leasing out, with a payback period of around one year. With a gigawatt of computing power built on Nvidia 's Vera Rubin platform costing around $50 billion, that implies the company is getting at least that much in revenue per gigawatt per year. This also lines up with Musk saying SpaceX could end 2027 with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of between $500 billion and $1 trillion.
If SpaceX were to add 10 gigawatts of new compute capacity each year, its "super intelligence" segment (formerly known as its AI segment) would end 2030 with annual recurring revenue of more than $2 trillion. However, it would need to raise capital to fund its capex spending, which I assume will start with 10% dilution and go down 1% a year thereafter. Actual results would vary based on its cost, capex needs, and share price.
Below is a potential scenario as to what SpaceX's AI build-out could potentially look like.
Figures based on aggressive assumptions by author.
Between its AI infrastructure business and the growth of Starlink, Cursor, and its rocket launch business, SpaceX could generate $2 trillion in revenue in 2030. If you speculate that the market will value the company at a forward price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 5 -- a multiple at which Musk's other public company, Tesla , has often traded -- the stock would be worth around $570 by the end of 2029. That would be a more than 300% increase in the stock's price in three years.
The biggest risk to the company hitting this revenue target, meanwhile, would be if compute rental prices fell as it brought more capacity online.

articles.title_orig: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.
The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.
Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.
The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.
Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

The IRS has released the 2027 standard deduction amounts you'll use for your 2027 tax return — and they're higher than ever.
The federal tax agency adjusts these amounts for each filing status every year. Since these adjustments are based on inflation, the standard deduction is higher for 2027 than in recent years.
Knowing the standard deduction for your status can help you determine whether you should plan to itemize or claim the standard deduction next year.

Married, Filing Jointly and Surviving Spouses
Increase of $1,000 from the prior tax year
Single and Married, Filing Separately
Increase of $500 from the prior tax year
Increase of $775 from the prior tax year
Taxpayers age 65 and older, as well as those who are blind, can claim an additional standard deduction . For 2027, that additional amount is $1,700 ($2,100 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse).
Those eligible can add the extra standard deduction to the regular amount for their filing status. A single taxpayer 65 or older (or who is blind) can claim a total standard deduction of $18,700 on their 2027 federal tax return.
Additionally, as Kiplinger has reported, the 2025 Trump tax bill introduced a new bonus standard deduction of $6,000 for those age 65 and older.
This can be added to the 2027 standard deduction for each eligible individual and can be claimed by those who itemize.
However, the "bonus" amount is temporary and phases out for incomes above certain thresholds.
Your standard deduction amount might differ if you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal tax return.
The 2027 standard deduction for dependents is limited to either $1,400 or the sum of $500 and the dependent's earned income, whichever is greater.
Note: The standard deduction for dependents cannot exceed the regular standard deduction for your filing status, even if your earned income is higher than the basic standard deduction amount.
Given the new senior bonus deduction, the existing extra standard deduction for those over age 65, and changes to the base standard deduction, the highest possible 2027 standard deduction amount is a whopping $48,600.
That amount is for married couples filing jointly who are both age 65 or older, qualify for the bonus deduction, and can claim the extra standard deduction for both spouses.
For more information on how to calculate your total standard deduction, see: The Extra Standard Deduction for People Age 65 and Older .

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 4, 2026.
As Democrats are celebrating a historic blue wave , eyes are on the Senate race in deep-red Mississippi, where the Democratic candidate led the Republican incumbent by a razor-thin margin of 1,138 votes as of Wednesday evening.
The Associated Press has not yet called the race because it is so close, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom ahead by about 0.1%—he has so far earned 49% of the vote compared to Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 48.9%, with 96% of votes counted. It’s a stunning nail-biter of a race that, in the weeks leading up to Election Day, polls had suggested would likely be won by the Republican incumbent by a narrow margin.
“I can’t recall the last time it’s been this close for a statewide Senate contest—or a statewide election in general,” says Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. “It’s unprecedented for [Mississippi] to be this competitive for Democrats particularly, certainly in the last 40 years.”
Read More: What Democrats’ Midterm Gains Reveal About Trump’s Voter Coalition
Political experts say it could take a few days before the outcome of the race becomes clear.
If Colom, a district attorney, wins the race, it would be the first time that Mississippi voters have elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. Senate since 1982. A Democratic victory would also be a remarkable shift in a state that President Donald Trump won by a nearly 23-point margin just two years ago.
Such an upset would cap off a string of staggering victories for Democrats, who have so far flipped seven seats in the upper chamber in this year’s midterm elections, including in other staunchly red states like Texas and South Carolina .
Both candidates appeared to be optimistic that the election would ultimately go their way, though they also acknowledged that the race is still too close to call. Colom said in a statement early Wednesday morning, “I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat.”
“The results are all trending in our direction,” Colom said in a speech to his supporters on Election Night. “The reality is, though, we’re not going to get the results tonight. I’m excited about our momentum, I’m excited about where we are.”
Speaking to a crowd of her supporters on Election Night , Hyde-Smith said she was confident that she would hold her seat in the upper chamber.
“We still don’t have all the votes in, so we’re not calling all of it tonight, but we’re in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator,” she said .
When asked about Hyde-Smith’s speech at a press conference on Wednesday, Colom replied , “Bless her heart.”
It is possible that the winner of the Senate contest may not be determined until the end of the week—or even next week.
The state has five business days after Election Day to count affidavit ballots. An individual would turn in such a ballot, which is also called a provisional ballot, in a situation in which they believe they’re eligible and registered to vote but are unable to cast a standard ballot—for instance, if their name is not in their local polling place’s records. These votes are only counted once election workers verify the individual’s information. Mississippi also permits mail-in ballots that arrive within five days after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by Election Day, to be counted.
All this means that it’s possible the race may not be called until a week after Election Day, says Emily Ommundsen, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.
“Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don’t expect any results to be called before then,” Ommundsen says.
The tight race in Mississippi is one of many that illustrate the extremely challenging political environment Republicans have faced this year.
Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in midterm elections, and that pressure on Republicans was compounded in this election cycle because of historically low approval for Trump driven in large part by the economy, as well as the war in Iran.
Ommundsen says that, while ballots are still being counted, the result in Mississippi, so far, “is consistent with trends that we saw nationally.”
“Nearly all counties that had a Senate election on the ballot moved towards the left compared to how they voted in 2024,” she says, though she notes that there are some exceptions. “Mississippi just happens to be one of those elections that was closer and perhaps more ripe for a flip.”
Hitefield likens this year’s midterms to “a referendum on the President,” adding that “Democrats were turning out to oppose the President and to oppose the President’s policies.”
But he cautions that the close contest in Mississippi is not necessarily a sign that the deep-red state is turning blue or even purple. It’s possible, he says, that Republican voters didn’t cast their ballots for a Democrat, and instead stayed home.
“I wouldn’t necessarily read in, long story short, to Mississippi becoming a Georgia—you know, being a fully competitive every election state,” Hitefield says. “But I think it’s certainly moving toward a state that you shouldn’t sleep on when it comes to electoral competitiveness.”
Hitefield also says that there’s a lot of “voter apathy” within the Republican party with regards to Hyde-Smith, and she hasn’t performed as well as Mississippi’s other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, in past elections. Wicker won his re-election bid in 2024 by a more than 25-point margin . Hyde-Smith, meanwhile, won her re-election fight in 2020 by about 10 points .
Hitefield adds that Hyde-Smith had some “gaffes” during the campaign, when she made some remarks about the rising cost of living that some voters felt were dismissive. For instance, when asked about soaring costs, including beef prices, during an interview with WLOX in February, Hyde-Smith applauded the passing of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and went on to say, “It is on everybody’s mind. It is certainly me at my house. And you know, you have so many proteins to choose from. And all commodities go through peaks and valleys.”
National polling ahead of Election Day indicated that an overwhelming majority of American voters felt that the economy was a crucial issue for them heading into this year’s midterms.
Colom’s campaign jumped on Hyde-Smith’s remark, releasing an ad in which people objected to Hyde-Smith’s comment, including one who said in the video, “Pick another protein? Sh**, I’d rather pick another Senator instead.” The ad racked up more than 7.5 million views on Colom’s X account .
Ommundsen points out that Hyde-Smith didn’t make many public campaign appearances in this year’s election cycle; one of the few appearances the Senator made was last week, when she gave very brief remarks at a rally the President held for her in Mississippi.
Hitefield says Hyde-Smith didn’t “do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign” in this election cycle.
“I think that it was a real mistake by her campaign, regardless of what the outcome looks like at the end of this,” Hitefield says. “Even if she does win, she didn’t do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. I think that’s something [where] if she does win, she’ll need to think about, moving forward, how to strategize more effectively.”
Colom, on the other hand, ran a “successful campaign” and generated “so much voter excitement,” Hitefield says—so much so that it stirred “this groundswell of hopes within the Democratic party that this seat could be flipped.”

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales fell 5.7% in the third quarter, compared to the same time last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 27 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 27 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due to a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

articles.title_orig: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.title_zh: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.content_orig:
An update has ballooned Nier: Automata’s file size to 366GB on Steam.
This is seemingly caused by a bug that has added the full game’s file size to the file size of each DLC. When stacked up, it means you will need 366GB of space to install the full game and its adds-ons, despite it only being around 50GB prior to the update being pushed out.
While initially suspected to be a typo on Steam , RPG Site has since tested this out and indeed found that Nier: Automata now requires 366GB of space. It’s likely the bug will be addressed in a hotfix soon, so it’s worth holding off on installing Nier: Automata or the new update until then. It’s also a handy reminder to switch off auto updates on Steam if you’re unable to revert back right now.
Some report that the issue is fixed on their end, but others are still showing inflated file sizes when they go to install the game or the new update. The store page still says that you just need 50GB of space to install the game. It only seems that you’ll be asked for the additional space when you actually attempt to install it after purchase.
Curiously, the update that caused this hasn’t even added much to the game, instead adding support for three new languages (Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese).
Unsurprisingly, the game is seeing some negative reviews come in, seemingly from those unable to play the game now that it wants to eat up so much space on their PCs. Right now, neither Square Enix nor Platinum Games has acknowledged the mistake, so it’s unclear when a fix will be rolled out everywhere.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.
Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla.
Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail.
“It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.”
Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit.
And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts.
SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans.
“I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose.
Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares.
The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions.
Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches.
SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year.
How AI companies spent money on the midterms
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.”
Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.)
Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country.
Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads.
Musk bankrolling group using AI to attack Talarico on AI
“It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said.
Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said.
Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how
articles.content_orig:
iPhone Duo has only been available for a couple weeks, but Apple keeps improving the product with software enhancements. The latest arrives in the iOS 27.3 beta via a convenient keyboard update.
If you’re one of the fortunate early adopters who managed to get an iPhone Duo on or near launch day, you may have noticed that changes keep arriving via software updates.
iPhone Duo shipped with iOS 27.1, but just a few days later iOS 27.2 arrived and added Apple Pencil support and Edge Light for video calls.
Now just about one week later, the iOS 27.3 beta has introduced even more changes.
Reachability lets you slide outer display content to the left or right to make it more reachable. And as highlighted by Beta Profiles on X , the keyboard has gotten an improvement too.
iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z
The keyboard refresh with narrower keys and smaller font makes it easier than before to type on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen, especially one-handed.
It’s a subtle difference, but one that early testers have found a clear upgrade.
By combining keyboard changes with Reachability, iOS 27.3 offers a noteworthy improvement to the one-handed iPhone Duo experience.

articles.title_orig: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
articles.title_zh: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
articles.content_orig:
Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you.
Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you.
Meta now lets you have voice conversations with your Muse AI agent in real time, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced today .
The feature has been rolled out to me, and I gave it a spin on the iOS app while writing this article. As you chat with your Muse agent, the avatar at the top of your conversation animates in time with the words that it’s saying. You can also change the tone of the voice by just asking your agent about what you want and letting it decide or by browsing through a bunch of options in the avatar settings.
In my brief tests, my Muse agent responds quickly over voice, though it occasionally pauses while it’s looking up information or checking something for me (like it would with a text chat query). It also animates what it’s saying well, though for my particular avatar, it’s been a little uncanny. I set my Muse agent’s avatar to look like Mark Zuckerberg as a constant reminder that I’m chatting with a Meta service (I refuse to be charmed by a Jolly! ), and seeing the digital Zuckerberg facsimile actually talk with me is quite weird. I also can’t get my Muse agent’s voice to sound exactly like Mark Zuckerberg.
Muse’s voice mode and expressive avatars are rolling out now in the US for the app, Meta says . They’re coming “soon” for Meta’s AI glasses and will also be available for its forthcoming Muse Charm gadget , which is supposed to ship this year.

articles.title_orig: Travelers busted at airport with over 3,000 tarantulas hidden away in their socks
articles.title_zh: Travelers busted at airport with over 3,000 tarantulas hidden away in their socks
articles.content_orig:
Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.title_zh: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A San Diego-based franchisee of Outback Steakhouse filed for bankruptcy on Monday, citing expensive food and labor costs and declining customer traffic.
Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, which operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations mostly in California, said it has been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic . The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Wilmington, Del., seeking relief from hundreds of millions in debt.
Cerca Trova also operates Outback Steakhouses in Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico but said that California’s minimum wage laws have made labor especially pricey for a majority of its restaurants.
More than half the company’s employees work in California, according to court documents.
California’s minimum wage, effective at the start of this year, is $16.90 per hour. Fast-food employers must pay a higher minimum wage of $20 per hour, but Outback Steakhouse is not classified as a fast-food establishment under the law.
Beverly Hills-based Fat Brands Inc. said in a statement that it filed for bankruptcy on Monday to restructure the debt it accumulated while expanding its company portfolio, citing ‘difficult and largely unforeseen’ market conditions.
“By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged,” Cerca Trova Chief Executive David Goronkin said in a court filing. “Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise.”
The company’s debt has increased from $269 million in late 2020 to $449 million this year. It has between one and 49 creditors, court documents said.
Outback Steakhouse is not the only full-service casual dining restaurant to face challenges since the pandemic.
Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy in 2024, after its disastrous $20 all-you-can-eat shrimp deal . More recently, the Oprah-backed chain True Food Kitchen filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and closed three Southern California locations.
Inflation and economic pressure have led more Americans to eat at home or turn to fast food for a cheaper option, while the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic has curbed customers’ appetites.
The cost of beef has also been rising, up as much as 5% each year since 2022, Cerca Trova said in court filings.
Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Cerca Trova was once the largest Outback Steakhouse franchisee, with 99 restaurants in 2018. As of June, there were 659 Outback Steakhouse locations nationwide, 544 owned and operated by the brand owner, Bloomin’ Brands. The rest are run by franchisees.
Bloomin’ Brands, headquartered in Tampa, Fla., also owns Bonefish Grill, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse and Wine Bar.
The company has thrived this year despite pressures on the restaurant industry, with shares rising 60% since January. Shares fell Tuesday after Cerca Trova’s bankruptcy announcement and ended the day at $10.23, down 6.15%.  The company’s market value is nearly $879 million.
The Scottsdale, Ariz.-based health food chain True Food Kitchen announced it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Monday and has closed 12 locations.
Cerca Trova, also known as Out West Restaurant Group, proposed selling its assets to Bloomin’ Brands for $26.3 million unless a higher offer emerges during the bankruptcy process.
“This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee and does not affect Bloomin’ Brands’ corporate operations, financing, or liquidity,” Bloomin’ Brands spokesperson Elizabeth Daly said in an email. “Bloomin’ Brands is participating in the process as a stalking‑horse bidder to acquire Out West’s assets and seeking to support operational continuity and protect the brand while the court‑supervised process moves forward. ”
Cerca Trova could not be immediately reached for comment.

articles.title_orig: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.title_zh: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.content_orig:
The two companies helmed by the world's richest person have had a rough two-day stretch on the market. Tesla ( TSLA -10.77% ) closed at $398.50 on Election Day, and by 3:08 p.m. ET Thursday, it was trading at about $342, down 14%, representing a loss of about $225 billion in market value. SpaceX ( SPCX -9.05% ) fell from $141.31 to about $125, down 12%, or about $227 billion. Together, that's about $450 billion gone in two sessions, most of it on Thursday, when Tesla fell about 11% and SpaceX about 8%.
To illustrate how steep the drop has been, SpaceX is now trading below its $135 IPO price from June.
Image source: Getty Images.
If you had to sum it up in one word: politics. Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, and Musk, a top ally of President Donald Trump, is a likely target. Speaking on the All-In podcast on election night, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said Democrats had signaled they would use subpoenas "to go after Elon Musk." In Texas, home to both companies, voters elected a Democratic attorney general for the first time since 1994.
But political sentiment isn't the only reason. The Nasdaq was headed for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday as investors dumped chip and data-center stocks, on fears that new leaders in Washington and the states could slow data-center construction. SpaceX, of course, is exposed: Last month, it committed to a roughly $40 billion lease for AI chips with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, with payments starting in the first half of 2027.
Adding to the fire for SpaceX, Wall Street is reportedly trying to sell off pieces of that $40 billion chip deal to other investors, with Goldman Sachs and Apollo leading the effort, according to Bloomberg on Thursday.
SpaceX made money last quarter: $2.79 billion in operating income and $4.4 billion in net income, though it's still $413 million in the red for the first nine months of the year. Nothing that happened in Washington this week changes its launch business or Starlink.
But the fine print, or at least the filing details, are worth noting. That net income included a $390 million tax benefit and a $561 million unrealized gain on its stake in the Boring Company, Musk's tunneling firm, and two customers made up about half of quarterly revenue. Even after the drop, SpaceX is valued at about $1.7 trillion, roughly 150 times its third-quarter operating income on an annualized basis.
Part of Tesla's bull case rests on robotaxis. On Tesla's October earnings call , CFO Vaibhav Taneja told analysts he expects robotaxis to make a real dent in both sales and profits in 2027, and the firm said the Cybercab was due to launch in Dallas this month. Musk told analysts Tesla will end up doing "a majority of all passenger miles on earth" -- "unless we are stopped by governments."
That caveat matters more this week. Self-driving cars depend on regulators, and Washington just got less friendly to Musk. Taneja also conceded that the robotaxi business hasn't yet reached its cost target of 30 cents per mile.
The two companies are also tied together. Tesla's filing puts its SpaceX stake at $2.87 billion as of Sept. 30, and shows SpaceX with a $729 million balance owed to Tesla, most of it tied to Megapack batteries still on order. Bad news for one tends to hit the other.
Not all at once. The political risk is real, but for now it's mostly talk. The new Congress isn't seated until January, and investigations take time. Meanwhile, a two-day drop of 12% to 14% doesn't make either stock cheap.
If you believe in Musk's long-term plans, this is a reasonable time to start a position slowly. Buy in small pieces over several weeks, and keep it a small part of your portfolio, because these are among the most volatile tech stocks you can own.
If you can only pick one, SpaceX gives you a launch and satellite business that's already earning money, while much of Tesla's value rides on robotaxis that are just getting started. And if headlines out of Washington would keep you up at night, it's fine to wait until the political picture is clearer.
